region: Northern Hemisphere; main lumber species from eastern North America and Europe
description: Maple is a pale, dense, fine-grained hardwood sold as hard maple (mainly sugar maple, Acer saccharum) and soft maple (such as red maple, Acer rubrum). It is used for flooring, cutting boards, furniture, butcher blocks, instruments, and turning, and fungus-stained 'spalted' maple is popular with turners.

hazards.summary: IARC classifies all wood dust as carcinogenic to humans, mainly linked to cancer of the nasal cavity and sinuses after long-term heavy exposure. This applies to every species, so dust control matters whatever you cut.
The UK HSE lists a decrease in lung function as a reported effect of maple dust. We did not find a primary study on maple wood dust itself, and the HSE sheet does not say which maple species.

Maple bark disease is a lung inflammation caused by breathing spores of the mold Cryptostroma corticale, which grows under the bark of infected maples (mostly sycamore maple). It comes from the fungus on diseased logs and bark, not from clean maple wood, so it mainly concerns people who fell, debark, or mill infected trees.

exposure_limits.note: 8-hour time-weighted average, as restated by OSHA

related_species_note: 'African maple' in some asthma papers is obeche (Triplochiton scleroxylon), an unrelated species; those reports do not apply to Acer.

notes_internal: Maple bark disease (Cryptostroma corticale) is a mold/bark hazard, not a wood-dust hazard; kept at level 3 because the original NEJM papers have no PubMed abstract to confirm diagnostic testing. Kespohl-2022 is partly a review and partly a test-development paper. Spalted maple: searched PubMed for 'spalted'/'spalting' and found only papers on pigments and fungal chemistry, no human health reports; spalting fungi (e.g. Trametes, Xylaria, Chlorociboria) are different organisms from Cryptostroma. Do not claim spalted maple causes maple bark disease. HSE-WIS30 'maple' entry is not species-specific; no primary source found for reduced lung function from maple. Absence of reports for a hazard is not evidence that this wood is safe.
